newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Albright criticises China on troop moves for HK.
newsitem.headline: Albright criticises China on troop moves for HK.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Sunday criticised China's decision to push 4,000 troops into Hong Kong hours after the British colony is handed over to Beijing at midnight on Monday.
Speaking to reporters she broke with previous caution and talked about the importance of Beijing sending the right messages as it moves to take control of the territory.
"I don't think this is the best way to start off," she said of the troop deployments.
On Saturday, Albright had studiously refrained from criticising Beijing's decision to send 4,000 troops into Hong Kong by land, sea and air just hours after the handover.
In Hong Kong on Sunday night, however, she said: "It's very important for them (the Chinese) to offer reassurances to the people of Hong Kong about their way of life.

"It's not so much what any agreement permits but it seems to me that what we're looking for are the kind of message that is being sent by what they are doing... The message that has come I personally think is not the best way to get started."
She said that during her Saturday visit to Ho Chi Minh City she had been focused on Vietnam and only since had she had a chance to think about the issue more and discuss it with aides.

The troops, backed by helicopters, ships and armoured personnel carriers, are set to cross Hong Kong's northern border at three points at around dawn on July 1, the first day of Beijing rule after 156 years of British colonial rule.

The U.S. decision to sharpen its tone on the troops issue followed complaints Albright was diluting the strong message of support for democracy she initially sent by deciding to boycott the swearing-in of Hong Kong's new unelected legislature on July 1.
After that decision was announced, U.S. officials said the American consul general in Hong Kong, Richard Boucher, would represent the United States at the event.

During a reception at Boucher's home, Albright said her refusal to attend the swearing-in of the Beijing-anointed legislature, that replaces a chamber elected in 1995, "sends a clear political message that the United States is and will remain a friend to democracy in Hong Kong and elsewhere".
She said authorising Boucher's presence "does not, as some suggest, dilute the message of American support for democracy".
Albright told reporters travelling in Asia with her: "I believe we have to protect U.S. interests", including $14 billion in American investment in Hong Kong and $24 billion in two-way trade.
On Monday, she is due to hold separate meetings with Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's future leader.
She will also hold talks with leading Hong Kong pro-democracy advocate Martin Lee and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said on Sunday Tung had told him he would schedule new elections for the legislature next May. Albright said the democratic leaders she had met also spoke about likely May polls but she had not yet heard that from Tung.
It was the first time a specific month had been mentioned publicly for the polls.
"From our perspective the sooner the better," she said.

In an interview with NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday, Albright stressed that "it will take its toll in U.S.-China relations" if Beijing reneges on promises to allow Hong Kong to retain its political and economic freedoms.
On the same programme, she also said it would be a good idea if China apologised for the bloody military crackdown against pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in 1989.
